claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an FCC matrix.
The as-built alloy has a fine microstructure.
The as-built alloy has inhomogeneous grain sizes and precipitate distributions.
Post-processing annealing or ageing can cause grain coarsening in this alloy.
Post-processing heat treatment can modify the precipitate distribution in this alloy.
Grain coarsening and changes in precipitate distribution control the rate and mode of elevated-temperature degradation.
Grain-boundary characteristics influence diffusion and interfacial stress accumulation.
High-energy grain boundaries act as fast diffusion paths for oxygen.
Annealing-induced grain coarsening reduces the density of high-energy grain boundaries.
Under oxidizing conditions, the reduced grain-boundary density promotes a more uniform and adherent oxide scale.
A more uniform and adherent oxide scale reduces stress concentrations and delays scale spallation and crack initiation.
In reducing environments, the heat-treatment-modified microstructure slows internal degradation mechanisms.
Relative to the as-built alloy, the heat-treated alloy will exhibit slower degradation kinetics.
Relative to the as-built alloy, the heat-treated alloy will exhibit less oxide-scale spallation and fewer microstructurally induced flaws.
The reduced degradation will delay failure or make failure less catastrophic during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
The proposed mechanism applies above approximately 800 degrees Celsius for exposures of about 100 hours or longer in oxidizing or reducing gases.
Outside the stated temperature and duration boundaries, other degradation mechanisms may dominate.
